their efforts will be in vain, and they will have no share in the Buddha-dharma. How tragic! Furthermore, it should be understood that...

To understand the essential meaning of the Tripiṭaka is to rightly weary of saṃsāra and joyfully enter nirvāṇa; this first requires understanding the dharma of correct causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*).
The links of dependent origination are themselves the Four Noble Truths: ignorance, volitional formations, craving, grasping, and existence constitute the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*);

consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, birth, and old age and death constitute the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*); knowing suffering and abandoning its origination constitutes the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*).

The absence of origination and suffering is the Truth of Cessation. By recognizing this, one destroys the externalist's false notions of causal conditions and the view that all phenomena arise without cause;
thus, one abandons various inversions and does not follow false conceptions or deviant views, but instead gains deep faith in true causal conditions.
Second, one must truly resolve the mind, being startled and awakened by the fire of impermanence that burns all things.
Those in the world who single-mindedly seek liberation must practice meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) without ceasing for even a moment, as if their heads were on fire.
Third, one must skillfully cultivate the supramundane path of concentration and wisdom. The distracted mind of the desire realm is like a lamp in the wind;
it cannot clearly illuminate objects. If there is concentration without wisdom, it is like being in darkness with nothing to see; therefore, one must skillfully cultivate both.

Fourth, one must thoroughly analyze all phenomena to break through them by observing the arising and ceasing of causes and conditions, thereby destroying all attachment, views, and conceptual proliferation regarding phenomena.
Fifth, one must skillfully discern the open and the obstructed: knowing that all phenomena of attachment and views possess the principle of the Path and Cessation is called "open";
knowing that all possess Suffering and its Accumulation is called "obstructed. Sixth, one must skillfully cultivate the factors of the Path. From...
The foundations of mindfulness, whether treated individually or collectively, extend even to the three gates of liberation.

Seventh, one must skillfully cultivate the aids to the path, namely the five *sthāpanā-citta* (stabilizing the mind), the shared mindfulness of objects, and the sixfold contemplation of dhyāna—referring to the eight recollections (*aṣṭānussati*):

(1) recollection of the Buddha, (2) recollection of the Dharma, (3) recollection of the Saṅgha, (4) recollection of ethical discipline, (5) recollection of generosity, (6) recollection of the devas, (7) recollection of inhalation and exhalation, and (8) recollection of death; as well as the nine perceptions (*navasañjñā*): (1) the perception of bloating, (2) the perception of decay, (3) the perception of being smeared with blood, (4) the perception of festering pus, and so forth.

The ten perceptions (*daśasaṃjñā*): (1) the perception of a livid corpse (*vinīlakasaṃjñā*), (2) the perception of a devoured corpse (*vikhāditakasaṃjñā*), (3) the perception of a scattered corpse (*vikṣiptakasaṃjñā*), (4) the perception of a skeletal corpse (*asthisaṃjñā*), (5) the perception of a burning corpse (*vidagdhakasaṃjñā*), (6) the perception of impermanence (*anityasaṃjñā*), (7) the perception of suffering (*duḥkhasaṃjñā*), (8) the perception of non-self (*anātmasaṃjñā*), (9) the perception of the impurity of food (*āhāre pratikūlasaṃjñā*), and (10) the perception of the lack of delight in all worlds (*sarvaloke 'nabhiratisaṃjñā*).

The eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa*): (1) possessing the perception of internal forms, one perceives external forms; (2) not possessing the perception of internal forms, one perceives external forms;

(3) the liberation of the beautiful, realized by the body; (4) the liberation of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana-vimokṣa*); (5) the liberation of the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana-vimokṣa*); (6) the liberation of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana-vimokṣa*); (7) the liberation of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana-vimokṣa*); [and (8) the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñāvedayitanirodha-vimokṣa*)].

The eight liberations (aṣṭau vimokṣāḥ), which involve the abandonment [of desire] and the cessation of sensation and perception; the eight bases of mastery (aṣṭāv abhibhv-āyatanāni): (1) possessing the perception of internal forms, one perceives external forms that are few, whether beautiful or ugly—this is called "superior knowledge and superior vision";

(2) possessing the perception of internal forms, one perceives external forms that are many; (3) not possessing the perception of internal forms, one perceives external forms that are few; (4) not possessing the perception of internal forms, one perceives external forms that are many; (5) the base of mastery of blue; (6) the base of mastery of yellow;

(7) the base of mastery of red; (8) the base of mastery of white; and the ten totalities (daśa kṛtsnāyatanāni), etc.: (1) blue, (2) yellow, (3) red, (4) white, (5) earth, (6) water, (7) fire, (8) wind, (9) space, and (10) consciousness. One must be well-versed in the eighth [liberation].
Knowing the successive stages, one does not give rise to overweening pride; one achieves a sense of shame and dread of blame, possessing integrity both internally and externally.

Clearly illuminating the Dharma and non-Dharma, one skillfully distinguishes between the false and the correct within the Buddha-dharma. One destroys all heterodox and external views; this is the ninth [requirement]: one must abide in patience.
Regarding the two thieves—the harsh and the soft: externally, one's own kin are the "soft" thief, while ill repute and foul rumors are the "harsh" thief. If one lacks patience, then...
When one is corrupted by internal patience regarding various attainments of the dhyānas and becomes attached to them, compassion arises; this is being corrupted by "soft thieves.
When one is oppressed by external objects, these are "strong thieves. Tenth, one must depart from attachment to dharmas (*dharmatṛṣṇā*).

If one gives rise to various wholesome dharmas conducive to the Path—whether belonging to the outer or inner stages—and the mind does not become attached to them, this is the essential intent. Second, the explanation of the common [path].

Regarding the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*): previously, with their inherent nature and shared objects of focus, one perceived only the principle of arising and ceasing, giving rise to true insight to sever the fetters—this was the "four aridities" and the crude method of deliverance.
Now, the four noble truths of non-arising take phenomena as they are to reveal the truth;

through the equal contemplation of the coarse and the subtle, all are seen as like illusions and transformations—this is the "four prosperities" and the skillful method of deliverance. This is the wisdom of the contemplation of non-arising, which is called the supreme object of mindfulness.

The objects of focus are called the "foundations" (*āyatana*). Contemplating the internal body, the external body, and both the internal and external bodies—all material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*), whether coarse or subtle—are like illusory transformations;

this is the foundation of mindfulness of the body (*kāya-smṛtyupasthāna*). Sensation (*vedanā*), mind (*citta*), and phenomena (*dharma*) are all of the nature of suffering; that which is of the nature of suffering is empty, and all are like illusory transformations;

these are the foundations of mindfulness of sensation, mind, and phenomena (*vedanā-citta-dharma-smṛtyupasthāna*). Furthermore, there are three types of mindfulness: those with intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), those associated with it (*sahagata*), and those as objects of perception (*ālambana*). These constitute the four foundations of mindfulness.

The distinctions between their respective stages are as explained therein: three types of persons alike employ the four natures (*caturvidha-svabhāva*) to investigate and dismantle the inversions of permanence, bliss, self, and purity, thereby awakening to and entering into non-arising (*anutpāda*).
The two vehicles (*dviyāna*) share with the *Tripiṭaka* [teachings] the cessation of the ashes (*bhasma-uccheda*) and the realization of partial truth (*prādeśika-satya*);

however, they differ in that the latter involves the analytical deconstruction of substance (*tattva-vibhāga*), representing a distinction in the skillfulness of their entry into the gate. Once the Bodhisattvas have seen emptiness (*śūnyatā*), they also see non-emptiness.

The spontaneous entry into the Separate and Perfect [Vehicles] is left to its own course. Third, regarding the specific explanation of the Four Applications of Mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*):
the practitioner looks up with faith toward the Middle Way Buddha-nature, yet because its principle is difficult to clarify, they must rely on skillful means.

By practicing the Four Applications of Mindfulness based on the wisdom of arising and ceasing (*utpādavyaya-prajñā*), one becomes an outer ordinary person (*bāhyapṛthagjana*) of the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*). By practicing the Four Applications of Mindfulness based on the wisdom of non-arising (*anutpāda-prajñā*), one becomes an inner ordinary person (*adhyātmapṛthagjana*) of the ten [stages of abiding].

Abiding in reliance upon immeasurable wisdom (*apramāṇa-prajñā*), one cultivates the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*) to accomplish the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*). Relying on similar non-conceptual wisdom (*anabhisaṃskāra-prajñā*), one cultivates the four foundations of mindfulness to accomplish the ten transferences (*daśa-pratipatti*).

Only upon ascending to the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*), where ignorance is partially shattered and the Middle Way is partially realized, is this truly the cultivation of the four foundations of mindfulness through actual non-conceptual wisdom (*anabhisaṃskāra-bhūtā prajñā*).
Here, however, we are discussing the path of teaching (*śikṣāmārga*), which refers to immeasurable contemplative wisdom (*vipaśyanā-prajñā*).

The name refers to the immeasurable objects observed by mindfulness. Regarding the "bases" (*sthāna*), within each stage there are three types of foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*): those of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), those of commonality (*sādhāraṇa*), and those of objective conditions (*ālambana*).

To distinguish them individually: during the ten stages of abiding (*bhūmi*), one cultivates the foundation of mindfulness of intrinsic nature; during the ten stages of practice (*caryā*), one cultivates the foundation of mindfulness of commonality;

during the ten stages of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), one cultivates the foundation of mindfulness of objective conditions; and upon reaching the first ground (*bhūmi*), these three types of foundations of mindfulness become fully differentiated.

The *dharmasmṛtyupasthāna* (mindfulness of phenomena) in its essential nature (*svabhāva*) is manifested as the *dharmakāya*; the *sāmānyasmṛtyupasthāna* (common mindfulness) is manifested as *mahāprajñā*;
and the *ālambanasmṛtyupasthāna* (object-condition mindfulness) is manifested as *vimukti*. The locus where sentient beings are tamed is called *vimukti*.
Furthermore, the *svabhāva-smṛtyupasthāna* is taken as *prajñā*, the *sāmānya-smṛtyupasthāna* as *vimukti*, and the *ālambana-smṛtyupasthāna* as the *dharmakāya*; these are not sequential.
That which is not transverse is called Great Nirvana. It attains liberation from form and liberation from sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness;

it is fully endowed with the four virtues of permanence, bliss, self, and purity. It universally shatters the four inversions of ordinary worldlings and non-Buddhists, as well as the four inversions of the two vehicles.
Fourth, it clarifies the perfect four foundations of mindfulness: these four are inconceivable in number—oneness is immeasurability, and immeasurability is oneness.
All are the Dharma-realm, fully endowed with the three truths and encompassing all phenomena; beyond the Dharma-realm, there is no further phenomenon.

Within a single station of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), it is non-dual and indistinguishable from the other three stations of mindfulness. All phenomena converge upon the four stations of mindfulness; this convergence does not exceed them.
"Mindfulness" (*smṛti*) refers to the wisdom of observation (*vipaśyanā*); "station" (*upasthāna*) refers to the objective realm (*viṣaya*). It is the wisdom that is capable of observing.
Illumination that is eternally tranquil is called the object contemplated by mindfulness; tranquility that is eternally illuminating is called the wisdom that is tranquil while abiding in the object.

Wisdom is tranquil while illuminating, and the object is illuminated while wisdom is tranquil. This single characteristic is the absence of characteristics, and the absence of characteristics is the single characteristic—this is the true characteristic (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
The true characteristic is the Single Truth (*ekasatya*), which is also called the Buddha-nature of space (*ākāśabuddhadhātu*) and is also called Great Parinirvāṇa. As it is said:
This is because object and wisdom are non-dual and undifferentiated: suchness as the object is suchness as the wisdom, and wisdom is itself the object.
To speak of "wisdom" and "the locus of wisdom" is to name them both *prajñā*. By analogy, to speak of "the locus" and "the wisdom of the locus" is to name them both the "object of truth.
Thus, that which is not an object is spoken of as an object, and that which is not wisdom is named wisdom.
It is also called the Samādhi of the Tranquility of Mind, and it is also called the Samādhi of the Tranquility of Form;

it is also the Samādhi of Illuminating the Mind, and it is also the Samādhi of Illuminating Form. Form and mind are non-dual, yet they are dual in non-duality; these two are provisionally named as such only for the sake of transforming sentient beings.
This contemplative wisdom merely contemplates the single thought-moment of ignorance within the minds of sentient beings; this very mind is...
This Dharma-nature, arising from causes and conditions, is simultaneously emptiness, the provisional, and the middle. One mind, two minds, three minds—these are all one mind.
This contemplation is also called the "all-encompassing wisdom" (sarvajñā).
This object is also called the "one perfect truth," the "one truth," the "three truths," and the "three truths as one truth. It is for this great causal purpose that all Buddhas appear in the world.
The World Honored One observes that within this single thought-moment, the ten realms are fully present: the form and name of the ten realms are called "body";
the sensation of the ten realms is called "feeling"; the consciousness of the ten realms is called "mind"; and the perception and mental formations of the ten realms are called "dharmas.
The dharma-nature of form is one form and all forms; all forms are one form. Sensation is one sensation and all sensations; all sensations are one sensation. Mind is one mind and all [minds].

Regarding all minds as one mind, regarding all thoughts as one thought, and regarding all phenomena as one phenomenon—taking the nature of wisdom as the object of contemplation, one contemplates the nature of form within the ten realms;
this is called the contemplation that realizes that within form there is neither defilement nor purity.

This is termed abiding in the nature of wisdom. Taking the nature of sensation within the ten realms as the object of contemplation, one contemplates it as the realization that within sensation there is neither...

That suffering is not pleasure is termed the locus of the nature of wisdom; observing the nature of the ten realms as the nature of mind is termed the observation that fully comprehends the nature of mind.

That the nature is neither permanent nor impermanent is termed the locus of the nature of wisdom; observing the dharma-nature of the ten realms is termed the observation that fully comprehends the dharma-nature.
That it is neither self nor non-self is termed the locus where the subject and object are joined in the designation.
This is called the contemplation of the foundations of mindfulness of nature (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*).

If one contemplates the ten realms as being neither defiled nor pure, illuminating both truths simultaneously, then defilement and purity are non-dual in their nature; this non-dual nature is precisely the true nature (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
This extends even to contemplating the phenomena of the ten realms as being neither self nor non-self, illuminating both truths simultaneously; self and non-self are non-dual in their nature.
The nature of non-duality and duality is itself the true nature; this is called the contemplation of the common foundations of mindfulness (*sāmānya-smṛtyupasthāna*).

If one contemplates this body, sensation, mind, and phenomena with objectless compassion and objectless non-thought—like a magnet attracting iron, tranquil yet constantly illuminating—then though there is no thought and no movement, one exercises great kindness that universally covers all sentient beings of the ten realms; this is the vow of compassion.

May it be vast and inexhaustible; this is called the contemplation of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*). Contemplating these three types—the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena—with a single-mindedness endowed with wisdom is called the foundation of mindfulness of nature (*dharmatā-smṛtyupasthāna*).
When concentration and wisdom are balanced and harmonized, they can assist toward the Great Way; this is called the shared foundation of mindfulness (*sādhāraṇa-smṛtyupasthāna*).
All compassion is called the foundation of mindfulness of objects (*ālambana-smṛtyupasthāna*), and the foundation of mindfulness of the single nature (*ekalakṣaṇa-smṛtyupasthāna*) encompasses all.
The nature of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) regarding common objects is also like this; this is the meaning of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*).

Cultivating these three types—the Shared, the Distinct, and the Perfect—four foundations of mindfulness all possess ten essential points; while the names are the same, the meanings differ, as detailed in those [texts]. One must go there to seek them out.
Regarding "mindfulness without error," the brief explanation for the Tripitaka Teaching is as previously stated. As for the Shared Teaching, it takes [the principle of] non-...

The *Vyavahāra-yāna* (Distinct Teaching) takes the wisdom of contemplation on arising as non-delusion; it understands that greed and sorrow are like space and unobtainable, and uses this as the method for subduing them.

It employs the three successive contemplations as non-delusion to subdue the world of shared residence (*sahabhū-loka*), the world of skillful means (*upāya-loka*), and the world of karmic fruition (*vipāka-loka*), thereby perfecting the immeasurable greed and sorrow [of these realms].
The *Anuttara-yāna* (Perfect Teaching) takes the wisdom of non-activity (*anabhisaṃskāra*) as non-delusion.
To mistakenly perceive the nature of greed and anxiety as being anything other than their true nature is an error;
only from the initial subduing through names and concepts up to ultimate subduing is there the true meaning of the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).

Is it not in this that the Tathāgata’s final injunction for the bhikṣus to practice the path by relying on the foundations of mindfulness finds its essential point? Therefore, herein we speak only of the foundation of mindfulness of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*) in detail.
Advancing with tireless perseverance and receiving the teachings on the mind and dharmas is likewise;
yet, one does not definitively state them to be impure, suffering, and so forth, precisely because these are what practitioners of the four teachings collectively receive.

If one grasps this meaning, then all dharma-gates—such as the five hindrances, the four dhyānas, the five supernormal powers, and the three insights—can each be explained through four aspects. Contemplate this, contemplate it!

Fourth, the permanent abandonment of the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*). This section has three parts: first, clarifying the dwelling place; second, clarifying the skillful means for removing the hindrances;
and third, the actual explanation of removing the hindrances. Now, for the first part:
one delights in staying in an *āraṇya* (wilderness), a quiet place, or at the foot of a tree; or one delights in staying in a mountain cave, or in the open air, or amidst refuse.

Regarding the locations for gathering: if one stays among burial mounds, by the banks of rivers, or in an *āraṇya*—which is translated here as "free from clamor and confusion"—such places are secluded from the bustle of the crowd and are fit for spiritual cultivation.
Second, the explanation of the methods for removing hindrances (*āvaraṇa*).
Having returned from his almsround, he washed his feet, set aside his robe and bowl, and sat down cross-legged with his body erect and his mind upright, binding his mindfulness before him.
Sustaining the body through almsfood, he forever severed the pursuit of worldly gain; by sitting cross-legged, his mind easily entered meditative concentration. Straight...
When the body is free from physical illness, the mind is free from perversity and inversion; when mindfulness is bound to the present, dullness and distraction do not arise.

This section on the three correct methods for clarifying the removal of the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) has three parts: first, a direct explanation of the rejection and abandonment of the five hindrances;

second, an explanation of the characteristics of removing the five hindrances through analogy; and third, a comprehensive explanation of the method for their permanent severance. This is the first part.
He abandons stinginess and does not dwell with it; he abandons ill-will and is free from resentment and envy, abiding in non-ill-will, purity, and constant loving-kindness and compassion;
he removes drowsiness and does not dwell with it, fixing his attention on clarity and maintaining mindfulness without confusion;
he eliminates restlessness and regret and does not dwell with them, his inner mind being tranquil, his remorse subdued, and his heart pure.
Having eliminated doubt and crossed beyond it, his mind is single-mindedly directed toward wholesome dharmas.

Attachment to and failure to relinquish the objects of the five desires is called stinginess and greed (*mātsarya*). Anger and harboring resentment toward disagreeable objects is called malice (*vyāpāda*).
Being dazed, lacking clarity, and having the faculties obscured by darkness is called sleep (*middha*). The scattering and agitation of the three types of action is called worry (*auddhatya*).
Dejection and despondency are called restlessness and regret (*auddhatya-kaukṛtya*). Doubt regarding the Teacher, the Dharma, and oneself is called doubt (*vicikitsā*).
These five factors are called hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) because they obscure and obstruct concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), preventing them from being developed.

To distinguish them individually: attachment is a hindrance to wisdom, for it dulls the intellect; aversion is a hindrance to concentration, as it is precisely a thorn to meditative absorption (*dhyāna*); and sleep... [text truncated]

Because the nature of the hindrance of sensual desire (kāmacchanda-nīvaraṇa) lacks capability, it prevents concentration from being one-pointed; because the hindrance of ill-will (vyāpāda-nīvaraṇa) obstructs loving-kindness, it prevents the mind from becoming pliant;

because the hindrance of sloth-and-torpor (styāna-middha-nīvaraṇa) causes the body and mind to be heavy and dull, it prevents the mind from being light and buoyant; because the hindrance of restlessness-and-regret (auddhatya-kaukṛtya-nīvaraṇa) causes the mind to be scattered and agitated, it prevents concentration from being one-pointed; and because the hindrance of doubt (vicikitsā-nīvaraṇa) results in a lack of right faith, it obstructs both concentration and wisdom.
Generally speaking, all of these are hindrances to concentration and wisdom. Next, the characteristics of removing the five hindrances are clarified through analogies.
It is, for example, like a slave whom his master grants the surname "Peaceful Liberation" (An-yin-tuo). The slave thinks to himself:
"Formerly I was a slave, but now I am liberated; I have attained peace and security and gained self-mastery, no longer being dependent on others.
By reason of this, he attains joy, and his mind is at ease and happy. Or again, it is like someone who recovers another's lost property and is able to successfully manage their livelihood through it.
Having finished repaying both the interest and the principal, there remained a surplus sufficient to support his wife and children. He thought to himself:
"I previously borrowed this debt to manage my livelihood and obtained interest;

now that I have repaid the principal and there is still a surplus to support my wife and children, I have attained freedom and no longer fear others. By these causes and conditions, he then attained [the fruit].
His mind is joyful and at ease, like a person who has long suffered from illness and, having recovered from that disease, finds their food digested and their body endowed with color and strength.
He thinks to himself: "I previously had this illness, but now I have been cured; my food is digested and my body possesses color and strength.
By reason of this, he attains joy and his mind is at ease, like a person who has long been confined in a prison.
Having safely escaped from prison, he thinks to himself: "I was previously confined, but now I have been released;

I have nothing further to fear. For this reason, he attains joy and his mind becomes peaceful, just as a person carrying much wealth and treasure crosses a vast wilderness without encountering bandits or robbery, arriving safely on the other side. He then reflects: "Previously, I carried much..."
Having obtained wealth from the wilderness, one now has nothing further to fear; for this reason, one attains joy and the mind becomes peaceful and blissful.
Greed is like a slave, subject to the驱使 (driving) of another; thus, hatred is like a debt, which must be repaid with unceasing retribution.

Therefore, sleep is like a chronic illness, heavy and preventing one from rising; restlessness and remorse are like the cause of imprisonment, for restlessness gives rise to remorse, and because of remorse the hindrance is formed, making it impossible to escape on one's own;
doubt is like being in a wilderness, as the mind is full of hesitation.
These three possess the method for eternal severance: if one does not censure the five hindrances, one cannot practice dhyāna; and if one does not attain dhyāna, [one cannot realize the goal].
The power of meditative concentration alone cannot sever the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*).

It is the same for a bhikṣu who possesses the five hindrances: like a slave in debt, long ill, imprisoned, or wandering through a vast wilderness, he perceives that his own hindrances have not been severed, causing his mind to be defiled and the power of his wisdom to be obscured. He then abandons sensual desires and evil states.
When unwholesome states are accompanied by applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*), one experiences joy and bliss and enters the first dhyāna.

That joy and bliss moisten and saturate the body, pervading and overflowing it such that there is no place not reached. It is like a skilled bath-attendant who fills a vessel with fine medicinal powder and soaks it with water;
when the ingredients are properly blended, the water moistens everything without anything remaining dry, yet without any being lost.
It is likewise for a bhikṣu who attains the first dhyāna: joy and bliss pervade his entire body, leaving no space unoccupied.
This is the first time he experiences bliss in this very body. Why is this? Because through non-negligence, diligence, tirelessness, and unconfused mindfulness, he dwells in the bliss of tranquility.
He abandons applied and sustained thought (vitarka-vicāra), and thus internally gives rise to faith; he becomes unified in mind, free from applied thought.
Free from directed thought and evaluation, he enters the second dhyāna with the joy and bliss born of concentration.
With this joy and bliss born of concentration, his body is saturated, permeated, filled, and overflowing;

there is no part of his body that is not pervaded, just as a spring on a mountain peak gushes forth from within itself—not from the east, west, south, north, or from above—and this clear, cool water from within the pool saturates and permeates it all.
Just as a pond is completely filled and overflowing with no empty space, so too it is for a bhikṣu who has entered the second dhyāna;
his mind is concentrated, and joy and happiness fill him completely and overflow. This is the second instance of attaining happiness in the present body.

He abandons that joy and dwells in equanimity, mindful and clearly aware, experiencing happiness with the body; he enters the third dhyāna, of which the Noble Ones say, "He dwells in happiness who is equanimous and mindful. He...

In his body, there is no lack of joy; he is moistened, saturated, pervaded, and suffused with bliss, leaving no empty space—just as, for example, the roots, stalks, flowers, and leaves of the *utpala*, *kumuda*, and *puṇḍarīka* lotuses, though they have emerged from the earth, remain moistened by the water within them, leaving no empty space that is not saturated.
So too it is for the bhikṣu who enters the third dhyāna.

Furthermore, having thus become detached from rapture, he dwells in pleasure, moistening and permeating the body with it so that there is no part of it not pervaded; this is the third dhyāna, the attainment of bodily happiness where one sports.

Having abandoned pleasure and pain, and with the prior cessation of mental distress and joy, he enters the fourth dhyāna, which is neither painful nor pleasant and is characterized by purity of mindfulness;
his body and mind are pure, fully suffused, and overflowing, such that there is nothing not pervaded.
It is just as if a man or a woman, having bathed and cleansed themselves, were to put on new, pure white garments such that there is no part of them not covered;
so too it is with a bhikṣu entering the fourth dhyāna: his mind is pure and pervades his entire body without any gaps or omissions.
Having entered the fourth dhyāna, his mind does not waver, nor is it lax, nor does it [associate with]...

Abiding in the immovable stage, free from attachment and aversion, it is like a house that is tightly sealed, plastered inside and out, with doors and windows firmly shut so that no wind or dust enters;

within it a lamp is lit, undisturbed by humans, non-humans, wind, or birds, its flame rising straight up without wavering or curving, burning in tranquil stillness. So too is it for a bhikṣu who has entered the fourth dhyāna.
There is no agitation; the mind is free from indolence and is no longer associated with craving or aversion.
Having thus abided in immovability, this is the fourth dhyāna—the sphere of activity where one experiences bliss in the present body. Why is this?

Because of heedfulness, diligence, lack of laxity, non-confusion of mindfulness, and because one dwells in the joy of tranquility. (Note: *tsì* [pronounced *zì*] means to soak or moisten; *tián* [pronounced *tián*] means peaceful and calm.)

For one who perceives that their own various hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) have not yet been abandoned— although it was previously stated that they have eliminated stinginess and greed up to the point where their mind is single-mindedly directed toward wholesome phenomena (*kuśala-dharma*)—
this is merely a rejection and abandonment, not yet a permanent severance. Therefore, by means of the power of applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*),
one must abandon sensual desires, evil, and unwholesome states to enter the first dhyāna, and so on, entering sequentially through to the fourth dhyāna.

Attaining joy and peace, the mind does not waver; this is the permanent abandonment of the hindrance of remorse. Furthermore, being free from indolence is the permanent abandonment of the hindrance of torpor.

Not being associated with craving or aversion is the permanent abandonment of the two hindrances of greed and hatred. Abiding in the immovable stage is the permanent abandonment of the hindrance of doubt.
It is like a well-sealed house, plastered inside and out, which serves as a metaphor for the absence of agitation.
The firm closing of the door and facing the parable represents diligence; the absence of sleep represents freedom from greed and hatred; the absence of wind and dust represents freedom from doubt;

and the lighting of the lamp represents the straightness of the flame without curvature, which—burning with tranquility and stillness—is a metaphor for the harmony of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), capable of giving rise to the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*) and the three types of clear knowledge (*tisro vidyāḥ*).
Furthermore, the absence of humans represents freedom from greed; the absence of non-humans represents freedom from hatred; and the absence of wind represents freedom from [delusion].
The metaphors of the restless bird for lack of sleep and the straightened arrow for the absence of doubt are fully contained within the sūtras, śāstras, and the *Dhyānapāramitā-anupūrva-dharmamukha*;
those who require them should seek them out for themselves.

This fourth major section demonstrates that concentration arises from ethical discipline (*śīla*), and it is also called the training in higher mind (*adhicitta-śikṣā*). The fifth clarifies the absence of...

The superior and wondrous untainted precepts (*anāsrava-śīla*) are also called the "precepts concomitant with the Path" (*mārga-sahagata-śīla*). While the term "concomitant with the Path" generally refers to the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) and the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*), here it specifically takes the arising of true untainted wisdom as its distinct characteristic.
The text further divides this into two parts: first, the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*); second, the three types of clear knowledge (*trividyā*).

Elsewhere, it is stated that the three clear knowledges and the six supernormal powers are collectively comprised within six dharmas, namely: the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*), the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), [the knowledge of the death and rebirth of beings], the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-jñāna*), the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (*kṣayajñāna*), and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*). Regarding the knowledge of past lives and the divine eye:

The excellence of the function of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*) is further termed "clear knowledge" (*vidyā*). Now, the supernormal power of the bases of mastery (*ṛddhipāda*) is separately divided into three;

when combined with the divine ear and knowledge of others' minds, they constitute the five supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). When the knowledge of past lives, the divine eye, and the exhaustion of outflows are listed separately, they form the three clear knowledges (*trividyā*).

Although there are differences in their classification and combination, these are all simply the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍ-abhijñā*). They are all called "supernormal powers" because, as stated in the *Śrī-mālā-sūtra*:

The spirits are named *Tianxing* (Nature of Heaven) and *Tongming* (Penetrating Wisdom); their innate wisdom shines through with unimpeded clarity. Now, first, regarding the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*):
having attained a concentrated mind that is pure and free from defilement, supple and subdued, they abide on the stage of immovability (*āniñjya-bhūmi*). From themselves...
When a mind arises within one’s own body capable of manifesting another body complete with limbs and joints and with no deficiency in its sense faculties, one then contemplates this body:
it is a composite of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) of form; that manifested body also possesses these four great elements of form.

This physical body is distinct from that manifested body, and the four great elements of the physical body are distinct from the four great elements of the manifested body. From within these four great elements of the physical body, a mind arises and manifests that other body. All [of this]...
The faculties, limbs, and joints are fully complete. It is like a person drawing a sword from its scabbard, thinking:

"This is the scabbard; this is the sword. The sword is one thing, the scabbard another. Having drawn the sword out from this scabbard—("she" being the sound for "scabbard," meaning the sheath)—it is also like a person taking a snake out from a basket, thinking:
"This is the basket; this is the snake. The basket is one thing, the snake another. From this...
A snake emerging from a basket (*kuaṅ*; *kuaṅ* is pronounced like *kuāng*; a square wicker basket): Suppose there is a person who takes a garment out of a chest (*dù*;

pronounced like *chén*; a tall bamboo chest). He would think, "This is the chest; this is the garment. The chest is one thing, the garment is another. As he takes the garment out of the chest, so it is with the bhikṣu.
This is the bhikṣu’s first supreme quality. Why? Because of heedfulness and diligence.
Because he is unwearied in mindfulness, free from confusion, and delights in tranquility, his mind becomes purified through concentration and he enters the Immovable Stage (*acalā-bhūmi*).
From within his own physical body composed of the four great elements, he gives rise to a mind that creates a transformation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*), complete with all sense faculties and limbs.
He reflects: "This body is a composite of the four great elements; that body exists as a creation."
This four-element physical body is distinct from that transformed four-element physical body; this mind resides in this body, depends upon this body, and is bound to this body.
It is like a lapis lazuli *maṇi* jewel, polished until it is exceedingly bright, clear, pure, and free of defilement.
If one were to thread it with blue, yellow, or red cords, and a man with sight were to place it in his palm and observe it, he would know: "This is the jewel; this is [the cord]."
Just as a string and its beads are distinct, yet these beads are strung upon that very string, so too it is with the bhikṣu:
from this physical body composed of the four great elements, he gives rise to a mind that manifests a transformation-body (nirmāṇakāya), complete with all sense faculties and limbs.
He then reflects: "This body is a composite of the four great elements; that [transformation] body arises from this, and this physical body of the four great elements is distinct [from it]."
That transformed body made of the four great elements is distinct from this mind; it dwells in this body, relies upon this body, and is bound to this body.

This is the second supreme dharma of a bhikṣu. Why is this? Because through heedfulness, diligence, tirelessness, mindfulness without confusion, and delight in tranquility, he cultivates with a single-mindedness that ranges from a pure concentrated mind up to the stage of immovability (*āniñjya-bhūmi*).
Having cultivated the knowledge of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), one realizes them and is thus able to perform various transformations:

from a single body one becomes many bodies, and from many bodies one returns to a single body; the body can fly through stone walls as if through empty space, passing through them without obstruction;
one walks in the air like a bird soaring, appearing and disappearing within the earth as if emerging from waves in water. Or...
Whether it be smoke or flames like a great mass of fire, or even the name of a grass (pronounced *zì*), his hands can touch the sun and moon, and his body reaches as far as the Brahma Heaven.
He is like a skilled potter who, having well-prepared the clay, can create whatever vessel he desires according to his will;
thus, he accomplishes what he intends and brings about benefit. He is like a master craftsman who is adept at working with wood, creating whatever he desires with complete mastery.
It brings benefit, just as a master ivory-worker, being skilled at working ivory, can fashion whatever he desires with ease and it brings benefit;
or just as a goldsmith, skillfully refining pure gold, can fashion whatever he desires with ease and it brings benefit.
So too is the bhikṣu: his concentrated mind is pure and reaches the state of immovability.
From the earth up to the Brahma world, acting according to his will—this is the third supreme quality of a bhikṣu.

With a mind purified by concentration, he enters the stage of the imperturbable (*āneñjya-bhūmi*) and, through single-minded cultivation, realizes the knowledge of the divine ear (*divya-śrotra-jñāna*).
His divine ear is purified and transcends that of human ears; he hears two kinds of sounds: those of humans and non-humans, just as one might hear within a city, a fortress, or a kingdom.
In a town there is a lecture hall that is vast, lofty, and conspicuous; a person with keen hearing standing within it hears various sounds without exerting effort in listening.
It is the same for the bhikṣu: because his mind is concentrated, his divine ear is purified, and he is able to hear the various sounds of humans and non-humans.
This is the fourth superior quality of the bhikṣu, attained through a concentrated mind.
From purification up to entering the Immovable Stage (*aniñjya-bhūmi*), he practices with single-mindedness and realizes the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*).
He knows the minds of external sentient beings—whether they have desire or are without desire, whether they are defiled or undefiled, whether they have delusion or are without delusion;
whether their minds are expansive or narrow, small or great, concentrated or distracted, bound or liberated, superior or unsurpassed—and he knows them all completely. This is the simile.
Just as a man or woman who delights in themselves sees their own reflection in water or a mirror without fail, so too is it for a bhikṣu:
because his mind is purified through meditative concentration, he knows the thoughts in the minds of all external sentient beings;
this is the fifth supreme dharma.
First, one initiates the mind to manifest a transformed body, like a sword emerging from its scabbard; these three successive metaphors illustrate that the transformation arises from the mind.
Next, one contemplates that the manifested body possesses a mind derived from that transformation, using the metaphor of a thread for the body and the metaphor of beads for the mind.
Thus, the body and mind are perfectly integrated, permeating one another through this transformation without ever being separated—these two aspects are inseparable.
These are all merely the preliminary expedients for the realization of supernormal knowledge (*abhijñā-jñāna*). Next, the actual manifestation of the realization of supernormal knowledge is shown.

Regarding the term "realization through knowledge" (*jñāna-sākṣātkriyā*): it refers to the supernormal powers realized by supramundane right knowledge (*lokottara-samyag-jñāna*), which differ from those obtained as a karmic reward by the various devas, and differ from those cultivated by externalists and ordinary worldlings based on views and craving.
The four similes of the master craftsman collectively illustrate how [the powers] function according to one's will.

If a craftsman’s technical skills can make wood harder than clay, ivory harder than wood, and gold harder than ivory—treating and utilizing them all as he pleases—how much more so should the mental factors, which are empty and harmonious, and the sublime path, which is subtle and skillful, not be able to act with mastery according to one's will?
Next is the knowledge of the divine ear, followed by the knowledge of others' minds; both may be understood according to the text. Next are the three types of clear knowledge (*vidyā*).

With a mind purified by concentration and having entered the stage of immovability (*āneñjya-bhūmi*), he cultivates and realizes the knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pūrva-nivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*).
He is then able to remember various kinds of past lives, numbering in the hundreds, thousands, and countless hundreds of thousands;
even through kalpas when the world-systems were consumed by fire and then regenerated, he can recall where he was born and what his name was.
He recollects such names, such lineages, such clans, such food, such lifespans, such durations in the world,
such ends of life, such experiences of suffering and pleasure, such deaths from that place and births in another, and such successive transmigration leading to birth here—
recollecting all these countless varieties of physical forms and appearances as if they were before his eyes.
Suppose there is a person who travels from his own village to another country;
while in that country, whether walking, standing, speaking, or remaining silent, he then travels from that country to yet another country, whether walking, standing, speaking, or remaining silent.

In this manner, proceeding by stages and eventually returning to his own country, he is able to recall and recognize all the countries he traveled through without exerting much effort. From [this analogy]...
From this country he goes to that country; within that country he acts in such a way, dwells in such a way, speaks in such a way, and remains silent in such a way.
From that country he goes again to another country; within that country he acts in such a way, dwells in such a way, speaks in such a way, and remains silent in such a way.
Thus proceeding by stages, he returns to his own country. A bhikṣu is also like this, being able to [act in the same manner].

With a concentrated mind, pure and even unto the stage of immovability, he realizes the knowledge of recollecting past lives, being able to remember various events throughout countless hundreds of thousands of eons.
This is the bhikṣu who has attained the first clear vision (*vidyā*); having abandoned the dharma of ignorance (*avidyā*), which gives rise to darkness, he now possesses the dharma of clarity.
This is the bhikṣu’s realization of the knowledge of recollecting past lives. Why is this so?

Because of heedfulness, diligence, tirelessness, an undistracted mind, and delighting in dwelling in tranquility, the initial knowledge of past lives is called the "first clear vision" (*vidyā*), as it illuminates the past. By eradicating ignorance (*avidyā*), the light of the Dharma arises;
when ignorance ceases, the afflictive obstructions of view and thought that obstruct emptiness and stillness are now eradicated.
When this is done, the Dharma of clarity arises spontaneously; it is said that there is only the method for removing the cataract, and no separate method for bestowing clarity.

Once darkness has departed and the Dharma of luminous understanding remains, it means that once darkness is gone, it will not return, and once clarity remains, it will not be lost—just as once pure gold is formed, it cannot again become ore.
With a mind purified by concentration, up to the stage of immovability, he practices single-mindedly and attains the knowledge of seeing beings die here and be born there;
with that purified divine eye, he sees beings die here and be born there— whether their form and color are beautiful or ugly,
good or evil, and whether they are in high or low, noble or base states— and he is able to know all this according to the causes and conditions of the karmic retribution created by those beings.
In this way, if a person commits evil deeds of body, evil deeds of speech, and evil deeds of mind, slanders the noble ones, and holds wrong views,

then by the retribution of those wrong views, they fall into the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals. Conversely, if such a sentient being practices good deeds of body, good deeds of speech, and maintains good thoughts of mind,
does not slander the noble ones, possesses right view, and cultivates right action, then upon the death of the body, they will attain rebirth in a higher realm.
With such a purified divine eye among gods and humans, one sees beings dying here and being born there;
one knows all the karmic causes created by those beings. It is like a vast level plain at a crossroads where there is a high and prominent hall;
a person with clear vision standing therein sees beings coming from the east and going to the west.
From the west to the east, from the south to the north, and from the north to the south— monks,

with a mind thus purified by concentration up to the stage of imperturbability, they realize through direct knowledge the wisdom that sees beings passing away from this life and being reborn in another;
with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, they see beings passing away from this life and being reborn in another, according to the karma each has created.
He fully knows the causes and conditions of retribution; this is the second clear knowledge attained by the bhikṣu:
having abandoned the ignorance that produces darkness, he has realized the dharma that brings clarity. This is the wisdom and realization of seeing beings dying here and being born there.
Why is this? It is because he is diligent, untiring, his mind is undisturbed, and he delights in tranquility through non-negligence.
Next, the knowledge of the divine eye (divyacakṣus-jñāna), which is called the second vidyā, clarifies the future.

Because it perceives all three periods of time and is able to foresee the future—which is difficult to perceive—it is described as preeminent; furthermore, it yields precedence to the knowledge of past lives (pūrvanivāsānusmṛti) and the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (āsravakṣaya).
With a mind purified by concentration, up to the stage of imperturbability, he practices with one-pointedness to realize untainted knowledge.

He knows the Noble Truth of Suffering as it truly is; he knows the truths of the Origin, Cessation, and the Path as they truly are; he knows the taints, the origin of the taints, the cessation of the taints, and the Noble Truth of the path leading to the cessation of the taints as they truly are.
Knowing and seeing thus, he is liberated from the taint of sensual desire and the taint of existence.

When the mind is liberated from the outflow of ignorance, one attains the knowledge of liberation, realizing: "Birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there will be no further existence.
It is like clear water in which wood, stones, fish, turtles, and other aquatic creatures move back and forth;
one with eyes observes them and sees the wood, stones, fish, and turtles, recognizing, "This is wood," or "This is stone."

Just as fish and turtles move here and there, so too is it with the bhikṣu: with a mind purified by concentration, having reached the stage of immovability, he attains untainted knowledge (anāsrava-jñāna) and realizes [the truths] such that he will not be born again. This is the bhikṣu’s attainment of the third clear-knowledge (vidyā):
the abandoning of ignorance (avidyā), the removal of the dharma of darkness once it has arisen, and the preservation of the dharma of clarity; this is called untainted knowledge.
It is explained why: because of heedfulness, diligence, tirelessness, mindfulness without confusion, and delighting in dwelling in tranquility.
Next, the untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*) designated as the third illumination clarifies the present; regarding all phenomena of the three periods of time, it is entirely...
Non-arising is so called because, having cut off the three periods of time through sitting meditation, there is not a single dharma that can be grasped by the mind;

therefore, it is called the noble truth of present suffering. That the three realms are all suffering is certain and not false; only the Noble One understands this, and thus it is termed a "Noble Truth.
Accumulation is the cause of suffering, cessation is the extinction of suffering, and the path is the essential means of escape—all of these are real and not false.

Therefore, all are termed *satya* (truths). That which is with-outflows (*sāsrava*) is the fruit of suffering; the accumulation of outflows (*āsrava-samudaya*) is the cause of suffering; the exhaustion of outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya*) is the cessation of suffering;

and the path leading to the exhaustion of outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya-gāminī pratipad*) is the means of escape. The reason for the repetition is that the first instance refers to the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), while the latter refers to the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*).

Alternatively, the first instance refers to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), while the latter refers to the form and formless realms (*rūpa-ārūpyadhātu*). This is called "correct knowledge" (*samyag-jñāna*).

The wisdom-eye is called "vision. The afflictions of deliberation in the desire realm are called the "outflow of desire" (*kāma-āsrava*); the afflictions of deliberation in the form and formless realms are called the "outflow of existence" (*bhava-āsrava*);
and the afflictions of vision in the three realms are called the "outflow of ignorance" (*avidyā-āsrava*).

One who attains liberation possesses the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) through the sixteen moments of mind in the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) and the eighteen moments of mind in the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*). The wisdom of one who has attained liberation is the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*). This is "I."

"Birth is exhausted" means that one is eternally free from karmic retribution; therefore, it is called the "Brahmacarya. "The holy life has been established" means that one is endowed with the virtues of wisdom and abandonment;
therefore, one is called an "Arhat" (Worthy One). "What was to be done has been accomplished" means that one has truly reached the end and all delusions are exhausted;
therefore, one is called an "Aśaikṣa" (One Beyond Training). "No further birth" means that afflictions are completely severed; therefore, one is called a "Slayer of the Foe. Furthermore, I...
"Birth is exhausted" is the perfection of knowledge regarding the Truth of Suffering; "the holy life has been established" is the perfection of knowledge regarding the Truth of the Path;

"what was to be done has been accomplished" is the perfection of knowledge regarding the Truth of Cessation; and "there is no further rebirth" is the perfection of knowledge regarding the Truth of Origination.

The concentration likened to clear water is the mind; the wood, stones, fish, and turtles are the phenomena presently arising; the eye is wisdom. Although one possesses the clear eye, [it must be applied].

Just as water that is not clear and still cannot distinguish wood, stones, fish, or turtles, so too, one who possesses wisdom but lacks concentration—even if they have clear water—cannot distinguish wood, stones, fish, or turtles if their eyes are not clear.
Likewise, one who possesses concentration but lacks wisdom cannot do so;

however, when concentration and wisdom are both fully perfected, one thoroughly understands the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) and the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), and does not give rise to delusion regarding persons or phenomena.
Inverted perceptions are eliminated by this untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*). This fifth major section concerns the arising of wisdom from meditative concentration;

it is also called the training in higher wisdom (*adhiprajñā-śikṣā*). Although in some places the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*) are still categorized under the training in concentration (*adhicitta-śikṣā*), here they are all termed "realization through wisdom" and are therefore subsumed within the training in wisdom.
Following the detailed explanation of the supernormal powers within meditative concentration, each concludes by stating: "This is due to non-negligence (*apramāda*)."

The phrase "and so forth" (ādi) profoundly reveals that maintaining the precepts and practicing heedfulness are the root of the Noble Path; the four foundations of mindfulness (catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni) are the essential gateway for entering the Path;
and the dhūta practices are the supreme method for renunciation. Thus, based on the Tripiṭaka, this has been briefly elucidated;
the remaining three cycles can be understood through one's own reflection. Furthermore, these very Dharma-gates of the Tripiṭaka may also be transformed and enter [other categories].
The subtleties, or the subtleties according to their respective positions, should be reflected upon in detail; do not overlook them.
This concludes the Brief Explanation of the Mahā- and Kṣudraka-Śīla-khandhaka.
